Enterotypes

Source: R/enterotype.r
enterotype.Rd

Clusters samples into community types as Arumugam et al. (2011) did for the human gut: partitioning around medoids (PAM) on Jensen-Shannon distances, with the number of types chosen by the Calinski-Harabasz (CH) index, and each sample's fit given by its silhouette.

Usage

enterotype(
  x,
  n_types = 2:10,
  ch = c("medoids", "centroids"),
  counts = NULL,
  margin = 1L,
  cpus = n_cpus()
)

Arguments

x

A count table (or proportions), from which jensen() distances are computed; or a dist object, such as one from beta_div(), used as it is, so that other distances can be tried. Samples are rows unless margin = 2.

n_types

The numbers of types to try (each from 2 to the number of samples minus 1); a single value fixes it. Default 2:10, cut to 2:(n - 1) for fewer than 11 samples.

ch

Which form of the Calinski-Harabasz index chooses the number of types: "medoids" (the default), as clusterSim::index.G1(centrotypes = "medoids") computes it in Arumugam et al.'s published script, or "centroids", the pseudo-F of the distances. See Details.

counts

Only with distances as x: an optional count table of the same samples (matched by name, or else by position), from which each type's mean composition (profiles) and top_feature are computed. Without it, a dist gives no profiles.

margin

If your samples are in the table's rows, set to 1L (the default). If they are in columns, set to 2L.

cpus

How many parallel processing threads to use. Results are the same for any number. Default: all available cores.

Value

A data frame of class c("ecodive_enterotype", "ecodive_types", "data.frame"), one row per sample (see ecodive_types), with columns sample, type (a factor) and silhouette. Its attributes:

  • types: a data frame, one row per type, with type, n_samples, top_feature (the feature of largest mean proportion), medoid (the medoid sample's name, or its position) and silhouette (the mean of the type's samples).

  • profiles: a types \(\times\) features matrix of mean proportions, or NULL for distances without counts.

  • selection: a data frame, one row per number of types tried, with n_types, ch, silhouette (the mean), objective (PAM's mean distance to the nearest medoid) and selected.

  • objective: PAM's mean distance from each sample to its nearest medoid for the chosen number of types, after BUILD and after SWAP, as cluster::pam() reports it.

  • ch: how the CH index was computed, "medoids" or "centroids".

  • method: "enterotype".

plot() draws the types' profiles or the selection (see plot.ecodive_types()); its title is "Enterotypes of" the distance's title.

Details

PAM (Kaufman & Rousseeuw 1990, ch. 2) chooses \(k\) samples as medoids, and assigns every sample to its nearest medoid. BUILD picks the medoids one at a time: first the sample with the smallest total distance to all others, then each time the sample that most reduces the total distance to the nearest medoid. SWAP then makes the best exchange of a medoid with a non-medoid, as long as one lowers the total. Ties go to the Types are numbered in the order of their medoids' positions in the input. Where samples tie, PAM breaks the tie as cluster::pam() does in nearly every case tested: in BUILD, the highest sample index; in SWAP, the first swap found; and a sample equally near two medoids joins the lower-indexed one.

The Calinski-Harabasz index compares the spread between types with the spread within them; the number of types with the largest index is chosen (the smallest, on ties). Both forms are $$CH = \frac{(T - W)/(k - 1)}{W/(n - k)}$$ for \(n\) samples in \(k\) types, with \(T\) the total spread and \(W\) the spread within types.

  • ch = "medoids" follows clusterSim::index.G1(x, cl, d, centrotypes = "medoids"), which Arumugam et al.'s script calls with the Jensen-Shannon distances as d and the samples' relative abundances as x. The medoid \(m_c\) of each type, and \(M\) of all samples, is the member with the smallest total distance to the others. The spreads are then measured by squared Euclidean distances \(e\) between the samples' proportions: \(T = \sum_i e(i, M)^2\) and \(W = \sum_i e(i, m_{c(i)})^2\). For distances given without counts, \(e\) is the distance itself; this equals index.G1() when the distances are Euclidean distances of its x.

  • ch = "centroids" is the pseudo-F of the distances (the F statistic of permanova()): \(T = \frac1n\sum_{i<j}d_{ij}^2\) and \(W = \sum_c \frac{1}{n_c}\sum_{i<j \in c} d_{ij}^2\), for types of \(n_c\) samples. For Euclidean distances, this is exactly Calinski & Harabasz's (1974) index. It uses only the distances.

The silhouette of sample \(i\) (Rousseeuw 1987) is \(s_i = (b_i - a_i) / \max(a_i, b_i)\), where \(a_i\) is its mean distance to the rest of its type and \(b_i\) its smallest mean distance to another type; 0 for a sample alone in its type. Values near 1 mean a sample sits well within its type; values near 0 or below, that it lies between types. Arumugam et al. checked their clusters with the mean silhouette, which selection reports for every number of types.

Distances. The paper used the Jensen-Shannon distance, the square root of the divergence: jensen(), not jsd(). The base of the logarithm doesn't matter, since PAM, the CH index and silhouettes are unchanged when every distance is scaled. Zeros need no pseudocount (\(0 \log 0 = 0\)); some published scripts add a small one (such as \(10^{-6}\)), which changes the distances, and so the results, slightly. Arumugam et al. used genus abundances, so aggregate features to genus first to follow them.

A caution. Costea et al. (2018), with the authors of the original paper, describe enterotypes as a coarse stratification of what is a continuous landscape of community composition, rather than discrete types. Check the silhouettes, and consider ordinations (e.g. pcoa()) alongside them.

Differences from cluster and clusterSim

  • Medoids, assignments, objectives and silhouettes match cluster::pam() (with its default pamonce = FALSE) and cluster::silhouette() to rounding, and the CH index matches clusterSim::index.G1(), as described above.

  • cluster::pam() numbers its clusters by their first appearance in the data; enterotype() numbers types by their medoids' positions. The partitions are the same.

  • Exact ties can still be broken differently: cluster::pam() breaks a few ties in its first BUILD step otherwise, which can lead to another, equally good, set of medoids.

Same names in other packages

None known.

References

Arumugam, M., Raes, J., Pelletier, E., et al. (2011). Enterotypes of the human gut microbiome. Nature, 473, 174-180. doi:10.1038/nature09944

Costea, P. I., Hildebrand, F., Arumugam, M., et al. (2018). Enterotypes in the landscape of gut microbial community composition. Nature Microbiology, 3, 8-16. doi:10.1038/s41564-017-0072-8

Kaufman, L., & Rousseeuw, P. J. (1990). Finding Groups in Data: An Introduction to Cluster Analysis. Wiley. doi:10.1002/9780470316801

Calinski, T., & Harabasz, J. (1974). A dendrite method for cluster analysis. Communications in Statistics, 3, 1-27. doi:10.1080/03610927408827101

Rousseeuw, P. J. (1987). Silhouettes: a graphical aid to the interpretation and validation of cluster analysis. Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics, 20, 53-65. doi:10.1016/0377-0427(87)90125-7

See also

ecodive_types, plot.ecodive_types(), jensen()

Examples

    # Types of iris flowers, from the proportions of their four
    # measurements (a stand-in for a table of genus abundances).
    et <- enterotype(iris[, 1:4])
    et
#> # Enterotypes of Jensen-Shannon Distance
#> # 150 samples in 2 types, chosen by the Calinski-Harabasz index from 2 to 10
#> #
#> # Types:
#>   type n_samples top_feature  medoid silhouette
#> 1 1           50 Sepal.Length 39          0.825
#> 2 2          100 Sepal.Length 78          0.821
#> #
#> # Selection:
#>   n_types   ch silhouette objective selected
#> 1       2 2000      0.822    0.0268     TRUE
#> 2       3 1630      0.565    0.0208    FALSE
#> 3       4 1310      0.549    0.0191    FALSE
#> 4       5  988      0.405    0.0175    FALSE

#> 6       7  796      0.3      0.0155    FALSE
#> 7       8  805      0.263    0.0146    FALSE
#> 8       9  739      0.261    0.014     FALSE
#> 9      10  647      0.266    0.0135    FALSE
#> #

    permanova(jensen(iris[, 1:4]), et$type)
